description: Senior Solution Engineer with 3+ years of experience in developing Java SpringBoot applications in cloud-based infrastructure integrating monitoring and observability.
summary:
What I developed ?
AstroVital is an offline health self-assessment app for astronauts on long-duration missions. A two-minute daily check-in, typed, dictated or photographed, captures vitals, blood sugar, sleep, exercise, nutrition, mood, radiation dose and symptoms. Each reading is compared with the astronaut's own preflight baseline, and explainable rules rate every body system Nominal, Monitor or Act now, with clear actions and a flag when the flight surgeon should be told. An animated, clickable body map, trends and a day-by-day mission replay make slow changes visible, while an onboard AI explains the day, detects combined anomalies, forecasts problems and answers questions without any Earth link. A daily routine with streaks and badges keeps measurements consistent.

How it addresses the challenge ?
It turns health indicators into a quick, visual assessment with guidance. It is built around NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, cites the NASA risk behind every alert, and teaches how to take each measurement in space.

Why it matters ?
On the way to Mars, messages take up to 20 minutes each way, so astronauts must catch and act on problems themselves. The same tool can help isolated people on Earth.
details:
What does your project do, and how does it work ?

AstroVital is a visual health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long-duration missions. It runs entirely onboard: rules, data and AI all work with no Earth link.

PPT Link: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1LL7HTtFGDq8aMMgktIdhQYAkeIH3ogCQ/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=106163910235626515775&rtpof=true&sd=true

It works in five steps:

  1. Log: A two-minute daily check-in records vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, temperature, body mass), fasting blood glucose, sleep, exercise, fluid, energy and protein intake, mood, stress, fatigue, radiation dose and 20 spaceflight-relevant symptoms. Astronauts can type, tap, dictate, or photograph a visible symptom such as a rash. A built-in reaction-time test measures alertness.
  2. Compare: Every reading is compared with the astronaut's own preflight baseline, not population averages, because microgravity changes what "normal" means.
  3. Evaluate: Nineteen explainable rules rate seven health domains as Nominal, Monitor or Act now. Each finding includes clear actions and flags when the flight surgeon should be told.
  4. Explain: An onboard AI writes a daily briefing, detects days when several signals drift together, forecasts when a trend will cross a threshold, and answers questions from the astronaut's own records.
  5. Act: Actions appear on screen, and a compact report is ready to send to Earth whenever the link allows.

What benefits does it have ?

  • Catches problems early: Slow declines in sleep, mood, body mass or alertness become visible days before they turn serious.
  • Works without Earth: Astronauts can assess and act on their health immediately, even with long delays or communication blackouts.
  • Explains itself: Every alert shows the data behind it, the rule that triggered it and the NASA health risk it relates to.
  • Respects crew time: One short daily check-in; routine tasks tick off automatically from the logged data.
  • Teaches: A Learn page and in-app guides explain how to take each measurement in space, why it matters, and when to escalate.

What is the intended impact ?

On the way to Mars, messages take up to 20 minutes each way and evacuation is impossible. AstroVital helps astronauts detect and manage health changes themselves, which reduces mission risk and gives flight surgeons trustworthy, well-organized data. Mission profile surface, a pressurized rover, Mars transit and the Mars surface, using published radiation measurements. The same tool can help people far from medical care on Earth, such as Antarctic research stations, ships, mines and remote clinics.

What tools did you use ?

Python with FastAPI and SQLite for the backend, and React with TypeScript, Vite face. The onboard AI is our own lightweight, explainable model set: a trainedintent classifier, a language extractor, and statistical anomaly and trend models. It runs on an ordinary CPU with no internet. We tested with pytest (44 automated tests) and Playwright, and produced the media with ffmpeg and pptxgenjs. Health content draws on NASA'ssources (5 Hazards, Human System Risks, Ongoing HRP Research) and the CanadianSpace Agency's radiation and ISS science pages.

How is your project creative ?

  • An animated, clickable body map: each organ is colored by status and explains ght affects it, and what to do.
  • A Mission Story that replays the entire mission day by day without hindsight, showing what was detected and when.
  • AI designed to live on a spacecraft: transparent, small and fully offline.
  • A routine with streaks and badges that rewards consistent logging, never "good" numbers, so astronauts have no reason to hide symptoms.

What factors did your team consider ?

  • Safety first: Deterministic rules control every health status. The AI explainsever downgrade an alert, and emergency phrases always trigger checklist guidance.
  • Offline operation: Works on one laptop without any network connection.
  • Privacy: All data stays onboard.
  • Accessibility: Every color has a text label, the interface works with a keyboard, and motion is reduced when the system requests it.
  • Honest limits: AstroVital is a prototype decision-support tool, not a medical are not clinically validated.

AI use disclosure: The code, documentation, slide deck and demo video were creatding assistant, then reviewed and tested by our team. The video uses a syntheticvoice, all demo data is simulated, and screenshots and video include an "AI-assisted (SI)" watermark. No NASA logos or design elements are used.
